explanation:
Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You would not be wrong to correct that picture if your mom and sister let people believe they’re very involved when they go months without seeing or even calling your daughter.

First, you’ve already done the work on your side: you kept bringing your daughter around and you tried multiple times to talk to them about spending more time with her. This isn’t coming out of nowhere.

Second, the real issue is your daughter is getting hurt. She’s old enough to notice the gap and ask why they don’t like her, and that matters more than protecting their image.

Third, they’re helping create a false impression by agreeing when people talk like they see her all the time and by posting photos that make them look more present than they are.

The other side might say calling it out in front of others is embarrassing or that their health and lives make regular contact hard.

You are the asshole for refusing to stop for your daughter’s birthday donut and turning the ride home into a lecture about her weight and calories.

First, she is 19, and this was a small birthday treat after doing a hike she mainly did because you wanted it. Refusing one donut was controlling, not protective.

Second, you made her birthday about policing her body and food. Arguing about whether the donut was “really” 350 calories and bringing up cake later was unnecessary and hurtful.

Third, there was an easy middle ground: let her have one donut, or at least save the health talk for another day. Instead, you escalated a simple request into a conflict.

Finally, blaming your wife as “enabling” makes it sound less like concern and more like you’ve turned your daughter’s weight into a family power struggle.

Your side might say you were worried about her health, but that doesn’t make this the right time or way to handle it.

You are in the wrong for telling your niece to “shut up.”

The specific problem is the way you want to say it. “Shut up” is rude and harsh, especially to a child, and it is likely to hurt her feelings more than solve the noise issue. Wanting a calmer birthday is fair, but that does not make it okay to speak to her like that. If her volume is the issue, the better move is to ask her politely to use a quieter voice or have her parent step in.

The other side might say it is your birthday and you want to enjoy it, but that still does not justify speaking to her that way.

1 — You were in the wrong for mocking your friend to force a response.

You made it personal: memes, calling him a clown, and repeatedly bringing up his sex life and his partner’s meth use to embarrass him. That wasn’t concern anymore; it was taunting.

You also had better options. If he didn’t want to talk, you could have stopped pushing, told him once that you were worried, or set your own distance from the situation. Trying to provoke him is what crossed the line.

Also, his girlfriend trying meth was alarming, but it still didn’t make it okay to turn her into a punchline or use her drug use as ammo against him.

To your credit, you apologized and admitted you were the one in the wrong, which was the right move.

The other side would probably say they get why you were worried, but your way of handling it was cruel and unnecessary.

Verdict: you are in the wrong here.

1. You were in the wrong for insulting him and then misleading him about the invite.

First, telling him to “f*ck off” and calling him an “annoying c*nt” was cruel and escalated things instead of setting a clear boundary. Second, when he asked directly about the party, you said “lemme see the list and I’ll add you to it,” which gave him reason to think he might be invited when you had already decided otherwise. Third, even if he is overbearing and pushes into spaces where he is not wanted, that does not make it okay to handle it with insults and mixed signals. A private, direct “no, you’re not invited” would have been more honest and less hurtful.

He would probably say he was trying too hard to fit in and that you gave him false hope instead of being straightforward.

0 — you’re not the asshole.

From your account, there isn’t a clearly blameworthy action here. You looked up from your phone and your eyes landed on someone who was standing right in front of you; that alone doesn’t show bad intent. Nothing in what you described shows you kept staring, said anything, followed her, or escalated it. And while the group reacted strongly, that reaction by itself doesn’t prove you did something clearly harmful or acted in bad faith.

The other side might say it looked like you were checking her out on purpose, even if that wasn’t your intent.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

You told your friend clearly that adding this new player was making the game less fun for you and changing the experience, and he kept doing it anyway. That matters because this was a long-running playthrough where you and your friend were already near the end, so bringing in someone far behind changed the pace and balance a lot. You also didn’t try to block them completely; you still let them use your server while you AFK, which shows you weren’t just trying to control everything. And if playing with them feels boring enough that you don’t even want to log on, stepping back is a reasonable response.

What the other side might say: refusing to play and saying you don’t like the new guy probably made things more tense, and they may feel you weren’t giving him a fair chance.

You are in the wrong for publicly talking about your ex’s penis size in front of friends.

First, that was a private sexual detail about his body, and you shared it without his consent. Second, it directly led to catcalling, jokes, and someone putting hands on him, and he was visibly embarrassed right away. Third, when he told you privately that it upset him, you didn’t apologize—you dismissed it by saying it was “totally different for a guy” and that you were “just trying to help.” That made it worse. Fourth, telling him to “calm down” after he was already upset was not respectful of the boundary he was trying to set.

He might say this wasn’t about the compliment itself, but about you exposing something intimate and then brushing off his feelings when he asked you not to.

You are not the asshole for wanting to send a polite text asking your new neighbor to turn the meditation music down.

First, the noise has been going on for multiple nights and is affecting your sleep, so this is not a tiny one-time annoyance. Second, you did not jump straight to a rude complaint; you even suggested a simple, polite message after trying to figure out what the sound was. Third, if noise from his apartment is clearly carrying into yours for hours at a time, it is reasonable to ask him to lower it. Fourth, waiting forever to catch him in person is not necessary when a calm text can solve it faster.

What may work against you is the “from Utah though” comment and the serial-killer framing, because that comes off as unfair and prejudiced when he has seemed nice so far.

1 — You would be in the wrong if you personally told your manager she smells.

First, this is a very sensitive issue, and the way you describe it includes humiliating guesses about her hygiene and period, which makes it more likely to come off as cruel than helpful. Second, you already know it could embarrass her, and because she is your manager, a direct comment from you could make the work relationship tense fast. Third, this has already turned into coworker gossip, which is unfair to her; piling on with a personal confrontation would not fix that. Finally, if the odor is truly affecting work, it should be handled through proper workplace channels and in private by someone whose role includes giving that kind of feedback.

The other side might say that if the smell is affecting everyone, someone should tell her so she has a chance to address it.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. She changed the routine, and blow drying her hair about 40 minutes before your alarm is a real sleep disruption. Being annoyed about losing sleep does not make you wrong, especially when this was not an issue before. You are also not demanding anything unreasonable if you ask for a small compromise, like waiting a bit when possible while you also shift your alarm a little earlier. And by your own account, nobody broke a promise or rule here, so this is more about working out a new routine than blaming anyone.

Her side might be that mornings are the only practical time for her workout and getting ready, so she may feel she is just doing what works for the household.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

Your mom made the hot dogs without you asking her to, and then blamed you for “wasting food” when the timing no longer worked for you. That’s not fair. You also told her you had just brushed your teeth, which is a normal reason to not want to eat right that second, and yelling at you over that was unnecessary. This really comes down to her assuming you were ready to eat instead of checking first. At most, you could have avoided the mix-up by saying before your shower that you weren’t ready for lunch yet.

Her side would probably be that she was trying to do something nice and felt unappreciated when you didn’t eat it.

0 — you’re not the asshole.

Your mom did go back on what she originally promised. She said they would cover anything the car needed besides gas, and then when the turbo repair came up, she tried to count that basic repair as your Christmas present instead. That changes the deal after the fact.

Your comparison was blunt, and raising your voice didn’t help, but that doesn’t make your main point wrong. You were reacting to a broken promise about a car expense you had already warned could happen.

It also matters that she raised her voice too, so this was an argument that escalated on both sides, not just you attacking her for no reason.

She might say the divorce changed her finances and that she was trying to help however she could, even if it wasn’t what she first promised.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not in the wrong for being upset that your boyfriend waved her over and then spent about an hour talking with her while you were left out. Being stuck there on your phone while the two of them chatted would make a lot of people feel awkward and sidelined. It also didn’t help that, when you wanted to leave, he called your attitude “pissy” instead of recognizing why you felt excluded. The bigger issue isn’t that he spoke to his ex at all, but that he let it turn into a long hangout without making sure you were included or comfortable.

That said, he might say you should have said clearly, in words, that you felt uncomfortable instead of trying to pull him away and then shutting down.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

Your concern is based on real warning signs: he’s underage, his cigarette smoking is becoming more frequent, and your family has a strong lung cancer history. You are not trying to embarrass him for one small mistake; you’re thinking about a pattern that could get worse. It also matters that you have only considered telling your parents, not publicly exposing him or trying to punish him. And the fact that you’re unsure and questioning whether it’s your place shows you’re acting out of concern, not spite.

The main point is that increasing smoking, especially with that family history, is not a harmless thing to ignore.

Your brother might say it’s his business, that he’s leaving soon anyway, and that telling your parents would feel like betrayal.

0 — you are not in the wrong.

You stepped up in a very hard situation and spent a lot of time helping your dad with supervision and meals when the hospital could not give him constant one-on-one attention. That is not causing the family rupture; it is trying to meet his immediate needs.

Your sister’s response is a big reason this blew up. Calling your caregiving “stupid” and saying she should not have to help because she would rather do leisure activities is not a constructive way to handle a dying parent’s care.

It also matters that, by your account, she persuaded your mom to stop helping, and then your mom cut off communication with you. That breakdown did not come from you asking for help; it came from them refusing to engage fairly.

They might say they are overwhelmed, exhausted, or feel the level of care being asked for is too much for them.

0 — you were not in the wrong for asking your mum to tell you upfront what time she can actually drive you.

First, your request was practical: if she already knows she can only take you at 8, it makes more sense to say that first instead of asking what train you want and then changing it. Second, this seems to happen regularly, so you were reacting to a pattern, not inventing a problem over one day. Third, what you asked for was simple and reasonable: clearer communication in advance so you can plan properly. The only part that didn’t help was telling your sister to “suck a cabbage,” because that turned a fair point into an argument.

Your mum or sister might say your tone came off sharp and that your mum is still doing you a favour by driving you at all.

0 — you were not in the wrong for explaining why the 200px icons looked pixelated when viewed enlarged.

First, your employer was rejecting work based on a misunderstanding of how small graphics look when zoomed in, so giving a technical explanation was relevant. Second, the issue was blocking the work, so you needed to clarify it to move the project forward. Third, you were explaining the actual size and display limits of the icons, not talking down to her just because she was a woman. Fourth, she ultimately forwarded the work to the front end, which suggests the explanation at least helped the process continue.

What the other side might say is that your wording matters: if “dumbed it down” came across as condescending, the tone could still have felt disrespectful even if the explanation itself was necessary.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You are not in the wrong.

First, you did not just shrug and ignore it from the start: you told your mom it was morally wrong to keep it from Cathy, and you brought it up again later. Second, this was never your medical news to deliver in the first place, especially to people you barely know; that kind of talk is better coming from the parent or the doctor. Third, once your mom did tell Cathy, Cathy brushed it off, which shows the real problem was not you staying silent. Finally, your choice was shaped by the fact that you had limited information, no authority, and no clear way to make them act even if you spoke up.

The other side might say that because the possible illness was serious and urgent, any adult who knew should have told Cathy directly no matter how uncomfortable it was.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not in the wrong for feeling uneasy about adding someone you barely know to a two-week international trip. A long trip is a big commitment, and it’s reasonable to want the original group asked before another person gets invited. You were also honest about the real issue: you’re shy, anxious, and slower to get comfortable with people, not trying to punish this friend personally. And you didn’t turn it into drama—you said she seems nice and that you wouldn’t let your discomfort ruin the trip.

At the same time, this doesn’t sound like anyone else clearly did something awful either. Your boyfriend’s point that there’s time to get to know her is fair, but it also doesn’t fully answer the group-consent part.

The other side might say that if she’s kind and there’s still time before July, giving her a chance could make the trip better rather than worse.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not wrong for being frustrated. A few things make that reasonable: your neighbour knows your work and sleep schedule, yet the daily argument with the upset child happens right under your bedroom window; it’s not a one-off, it’s a repeated and predictable disruption that wakes you two hours early; and repeated sleep interruption would wear on most people, even if 7 a.m. is normal for the area. At the same time, there are practical steps on your side too: since you know it happens every morning, closing the window before bed would likely help, and if it keeps bothering you, calmly speaking to the neighbour is more useful than stewing in it.

The other side would probably say 7 a.m. is a normal time to leave with small kids and that morning tantrums are hard to control.

1 — you’re in the wrong for usually driving well above the speed limit and using the right lane to fly past people.

First, by your own description, this is not an occasional mistake; you “usually” speed, and that is a basic traffic rule you are choosing to ignore. Second, you are picking the lane that feels most open so you can maintain that speed, even though slowing down is the obvious safer option. Third, the right lane has merging traffic, and passing fast there makes things harder for people entering and for drivers who do not expect someone coming up that quickly on that side. Fourth, your boyfriend’s point was about safety, not control, so this was a fair concern raised in good faith.

The other side might say other drivers should keep right and merge better, but that does not make your speeding and right-side passing okay.

1 — you were in the wrong for tracking her down off the app and telling her parents about her dating profile.

First, you took private dating activity and exposed it to her family without her consent. That is a major privacy violation. Second, seeing that she had a disability did not give you the right to decide she should not be dating or that her parents needed to step in. Third, you had better options: you could have ended contact, unmatched, or reported any real safety concern to the site. Fourth, the three-month ban strongly suggests you crossed a clear boundary the platform takes seriously.

The other side might say you were worried about her judgment or safety, but that still did not make it your place to go around her and contact her parents.

You are in the wrong for saying you’d go to the 11am ceremony and come home, then staying until midnight on your anniversary without updating your wife.

First, you made a clear plan with her, and you broke it by a huge margin. Second, even if service inside was bad, it was reasonable to step outside at some point and check your phone or send a quick message. Third, your wife had no idea where you were for hours, so of course she was worried and upset. Fourth, she even tried calling a mutual friend because you had gone completely silent.

From her side, she’d probably say this was not really about one missed text, but about being left alone on your anniversary with the kids while you ignored the plan and left her guessing all day.

1 — You would be in the wrong for inviting your brother but telling him not to bring his husband.

First, you are singling out his actual spouse while giving other guests plus-ones, and that is an obvious insult. Second, the problem you described is your fiancé’s family’s homophobia, not anything your brother or his husband has done. Third, you are putting the cost of “keeping the peace” on the gay couple instead of on the relatives who might behave badly. Fourth, excluding a husband of three years because other guests are prejudiced treats their marriage as less valid than everyone else’s relationship.

If you know some relatives may cause a scene, the fair answer is to set rules with those relatives or reconsider inviting them, not to exclude the person most likely to be targeted.

What the other side might say: they may argue it’s your wedding and you want a smooth day, but that still doesn’t make it fair to punish your brother and his husband for other people’s homophobia.

Yes — you were in the wrong for telling your wife to wait and then pushing a home metal-detector check instead of getting your toddler promptly evaluated for a possible swallowed coin.

First, with a young child, a suspected coin swallow is exactly the kind of thing that can turn serious fast, even if he seemed fine in the moment. Second, your plan depended on a DIY test that was not the standard way to rule out danger, and the doctor visit confirmed there really was a nickel. Third, the cost is frustrating, but saving money is not the main issue when the question is whether your child has an object stuck inside him. Fourth, your wife was responding to a real safety concern, so dismissing that concern made the situation worse.

Your wife may still have been wrong to call you “an ass” instead of just saying no and taking him in.

1 — You were in the wrong for knocking over and breaking equipment and supplies at work.

First, your frustration about being kept late on your birthday makes sense, but breaking a microwave, a toaster, and boxes of bowls and lids crossed the line from upset to destructive. Second, you escalated things by arguing about your coworker’s injury and then acting out physically, which made the situation worse instead of addressing the scheduling problem. Third, based on what you described, there’s no clear sign the waitress was faking or acting badly; if she said she couldn’t walk and might need stitches after getting glass in her foot, that had to be taken seriously. Finally, being treated unfairly at work does not make it okay to damage property.

The other side would probably say they handled an injury as it came up, but your reaction created a separate problem that you were responsible for.

1 — You were in the wrong for taking your niece’s keychain without permission, especially after she already took it back once.

First, it was her gift, not yours, and “she doesn’t need it” doesn’t make it okay to take it. Second, you went through her things, threw out items, and took the keychain from deep in a pouch, which crossed a clear line. Third, you had other options: ask her, ask your sister for help finding a cheap replacement, or tie your key to something else. Taking the same item twice made this about disrespect, not need. Fourth, bringing up money or snacks you offered before does not give you a claim over her property.

She was also wrong to yell and throw your key, but that does not change that you started this by taking something that wasn’t yours.

1 — you were in the wrong for taking on unpaid extra work in secret and then bringing that sacrifice up to your ex in an argument.

First, you made a big relationship decision without telling her, even though it directly affected how much time and energy you had in the present. Second, the plan actually made the distance problem worse for a while, because the extra work meant even less time together before the holiday happened. Third, once you used it after the breakup, it stopped being a gift and started sounding like guilt: “I did this for you, so you should have valued it.”  
And yes, you did make a real effort to create more time together, but effort you choose on your own doesn’t automatically become something the other person owes you appreciation for.

From her side, she’d probably say she never agreed to this plan, didn’t know about it, and felt blamed for a sacrifice she didn’t ask for.

0 — you were not in the wrong.

Your brother put his hands around your waist and buried his face between your shoulder and breast without asking, and you had every right to pull him off you. That kind of contact can feel very intrusive, even if he was just scared. Your reaction was sudden because you were startled and uncomfortable, not because you were trying to be cruel. Also, your twin saying you overreacted did not help; the better response would have been to calm your younger brother down without acting like your boundaries did not matter.

What the other side might say is that he is 13, got frightened by the movie, and was looking for comfort, so your shove and wording probably embarrassed him.

You are the asshole for choosing a concert trip over being there for your daughter’s 12th birthday.

First, your own reasoning makes the priority clear: you said there will be other birthdays, but no other concerts like this one. That tells your daughter the event matters more than she does. Second, this is not an unavoidable work trip or emergency; it’s a discretionary trip you can control. Third, your daughters gave you a reasonable compromise: go later or come back earlier, still see part of the series, and be there on her actual birthday. You rejected that because you want all three days, which makes this a choice. Fourth, turning 12 may not seem huge to you, but kids remember when a parent decides not to show up.

They might say you can celebrate later and that this is a rare experience with your son, but that does not erase missing the day itself when you had another option.

You are in the wrong for sending that profane text to the store and then pushing for the free pizza anyway.

First, they canceled your order and refunded you, which was frustrating, but your reply crossed the line into abuse. Being angry about bad service does not make “load of fucking bullshit” okay to send to workers.

Second, when you went in later, the employee did try to help by checking the system and asking a supervisor when nothing showed up. That was not shady on its own.

Third, once the supervisor explained that the deal was being refused because of your message, arguing at the counter just made the situation worse. The free pizza was a goodwill offer, not something you were owed after cursing at them.

The other side would say they handled the cancellation badly, but they still refunded you, and your own message is the reason they withdrew the extra offer.

0 — you’re not in the wrong.

You told him clearly that this is not just general shyness, but anxiety tied to a specific fear: that this friend is close to his ex and could carry things back. That’s a real boundary to have.

You also didn’t blow up or forbid anything; you just said you don’t want to meet them right now. That’s different from trying to control his friendships.

And after you explained why, he kept trying to convince you anyway. His reassurances may be well meant, but they don’t erase your discomfort, and “she doesn’t hate you” isn’t the same as you feeling safe.

To be fair, he might say he’s trying in good faith to include you in his life and help you feel more comfortable around people important to him.

1 — you were in the wrong for telling your boss a misleading story that could damage this person’s chance at the job.

First, you were not just an observer here: you were part of the emotional affair and even tried to make it physical, so presenting the other person as “the cheater” hid your own role. Second, you implied you knew this through someone else, which made your claim sound more objective than it was. Third, your discomfort was personal, not work-related, so using it to influence hiring crossed a line. Fourth, your version could unfairly hurt their reputation even though your own account does not clearly show they broke a commitment the way you did.

The other side would probably say you were trying to avoid a messy workplace situation, but that still did not make it okay to mislead your boss.

1 — You were in the wrong for knowingly putting false bedroom and bathroom numbers into the app to get a shorter booking.

First, the cleaner accepted the job based on the size you listed, so the booking was made on inaccurate information from the start. Second, showing the extra rooms only after he arrived changed the scope of the job in a way he did not agree to upfront, even if you said he did not have to finish everything. Third, the app uses room count to set time and expectations, and you worked around that on purpose instead of booking honestly and then directing him to focus downstairs. Fourth, the fact that downstairs took less time does not undo the misleading listing.

The cleaner could have handled it more calmly, but he would likely say he was upset because you set up the job with details you knew were not true.

0 — you’re not the asshole.

It’s reasonable to dislike people posting the same meme across multiple subreddits when it clogs your feed with the same thing two or three times. If you follow several meme communities, that repeated cross-posting can feel like low-effort spam rather than new content. You’re also not wrong for thinking people shouldn’t do it just to chase more views, especially when it makes the experience worse for people who follow those spaces.

That said, simply not liking it is different from being in the wrong. Your annoyance makes sense because the repetition affects your own feed directly.

The other side would probably say they’re just trying to reach different audiences, and not everyone follows all the same subreddits.

1 — You would be in the wrong if you brought your kids to Christmas only four days after they were diagnosed with the flu.

First, the flu is still contagious for several days even when treatment has started, so “no fever” does not mean “safe to attend.”  
Second, family gatherings are exactly the kind of place where one sick person can spread it to a lot of people fast, including older relatives or anyone with health issues. Third, your sister already made it clear she does not want to risk exposure, and pushing to attend anyway would ignore that boundary. Fourth, once you knew they were diagnosed that close to the event, the safest choice was to plan to stay home rather than hope they’d be fine in time.

The other side would probably say you were going by the fever rule and did not mean to expose anyone on purpose, but it still would have been the wrong call.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. Your friend was the one out of line here, not you.

First, it’s your home and you were not cutting people off from emergencies or basic contact, since everyone had normal phone service and data. Second, the real issue was your friend repeatedly ranting about it and then turning one guest’s casual comment into a public scene at your party. Third, it got tense enough that another guest stepped in with a hotspot just to calm things down, which says a lot about who was making the night uncomfortable. Finally, you listened to the feedback, admitted you hadn’t communicated well, and already decided to consider guest wifi going forward, which is a reasonable response.

The other side might say wifi is a normal courtesy now and that your rule felt unnecessarily rigid or odd to guests.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not the asshole for being upset that you came home after a brutal workday and 23-hour drive to no dinner, undone dishes, and being told to cook when the stay-at-home arrangement was supposed to cover that stuff. She had agreed to handle the home and kids while you were away, so your frustration was reasonable. It also makes sense that being exhausted and seeing chores half-done pushed you over the edge. And when she answered by saying you were “being an ass” because you’re gone, that added fuel instead of addressing the problem.

That said, calling her a lazy female dog and dragging the moving issue into the fight made it worse, even if you regret it.

Her side would be that early pregnancy, morning sickness, and handling two kids alone can leave her overwhelmed, so she may feel you judged her at her worst moment.

Verdict: you are not in the wrong here.

0. You’re not in the wrong for pulling back from plans when being around them leaves you feeling worse, especially when they keep making jokes at your expense about your school and living situation. That kind of repeated teasing can wear you down, and it makes sense that you’d stop wanting to put yourself in that position. You’re also not wrong for understanding why they’ve stopped inviting you as much; that’s a consequence of the pattern, but it doesn’t make you the bad guy. The bigger issue is that these friendships don’t sound very kind or supportive right now.

They might say the constant cancelling is frustrating and that they can’t count on you if you keep saying yes first.

YTA. You were wrong to call Sally and tell her to stop parenting your kids, to object to her helping at school, and to say her parents should not be involved.

First, she is doing day-to-day care for the children in the home they live in: meals, reading, school help, transport, photos, and even financial help. That is parenting in practice, even if you are still their mother.

Second, your complaint was not about a specific crossed line. You tried to shut down all involvement, including normal school contact and family support, which only hurt her and made co-parenting harder.

Third, there was a better way to handle this. If you had concerns about names, roles, or boundaries, you could have talked calmly and set clear limits instead of attacking someone who has been helping raise them.

From their side, they would say Sally stepped up in good faith for children who need stable care, not to replace you.

You are not the asshole.

This was a long-standing, serious issue in your relationship, and she knew that before getting the first tattoo and before booking the second. It makes sense that this would hurt your trust and feelings, especially because it was not a surprise preference you suddenly invented. You also are allowed to say clearly that you do not want a partner with more tattoos and to ask for a real conversation about what that means for the relationship. The bigger problem here is that she raised it once, dropped the discussion, and then booked the appointment anyway, which avoids dealing honestly with a known conflict.

That said, your point is strongest when you focus on your boundary and the broken communication, not on examples from friends getting “meaningless” tattoos later.

Her side would be that it is her body, and asking her to cancel puts pressure on a personal choice she feels should be hers alone.

You are not in the wrong.

Wanting a little extra safety on a first date is reasonable, especially with someone you only know from an app. You already took basic precautions by checking his selfies and talking through your sister’s concerns instead of ignoring them. You’re also aware that having Janna shadow the date could affect the vibe, which shows you’re thinking about Greg and the plans, not just yourself. And based on what you wrote, Greg hasn’t actually done anything wrong, so this is about caution, not punishment.

Greg might say that a shadow date feels awkward or makes it seem like he’s being treated with suspicion before he’s done anything.

0 — you are not in the wrong for wanting to speak up about child labour and environmental harm.

Those are serious issues, and it makes sense to object to a company benefiting from exploitative supply chains and poor environmental practices. Her bragging about wealth also adds to why this feels especially ugly to you. At the same time, a workplace award night is probably the wrong setting if your goal is to be fair or effective, because it puts your SO in an awkward position and turns a serious issue into a public scene. It also matters that, from what you’ve said, you know she heads the company, but not whether she personally chose or even knew about the specific factory practices.

The other side might say that confronting her there would feel more like a personal attack at someone else’s event than a real attempt to address the problem.
